This occupation is a U.S. military occupation, and O*NET explicitly does not collect military occupational data, so this page has no citable task frequency, work context percentages, interest codes, preparation levels, or wage and employment figures; before comparing positions or development paths, first check the establishment, specialty, training, appointment, and authorization rules of one's own service.

Validate with one paper exercise: you are given a completely fictitious tactical operations mission description (mission type and objective, team composition and specialty personnel mix, specialty equipment and equipment status, available communications and support means, terrain and time-of-day conditions, and interfaces with higher headquarters and support units). You are asked to write out the pre-mission preparation and briefing key points, team assignments and handover key points, the situation that must be continuously tracked and how to judge anomalies during operations, and the escalation targets and sequence when anomalies occur, and to mark which decisions must be made by personnel holding command authority.

Signals worth considering more: willingness to verify repeatedly according to procedures and standards, ability to mark gaps rather than guess when information is incomplete, ability to maintain record and handover quality during high-intensity and long-duration missions, and willingness to be responsible for the standards compliance of team members. Signals requiring caution: treating the military image or film scenes as the main content of daily life, unwillingness to bear review and personnel management duties, and a tendency to omit records or avoid escalation under pressure.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute recruitment, appointment, authorization, security clearance, or position competency conclusions.

First judge whether you are willing to work long term in a role centered on team mission supervision and coordination: it requires repeated verification and recording according to service standards, supervising the specialty team during operations and escalating anomalies within authorization, and being responsible for personnel specialty training and qualification compliance; validate with the paper exercise and seven-day task on this page.

The work of first-line supervisors of all other tactical operations specialists revolves around the cycle of “pre-mission preparation—team assignments and briefing—operation execution and situation tracking—anomaly determination and escalation—post-mission review and records—training and qualification verification”. Before a mission, check the mission description, specialty equipment and equipment status, and personnel specialty and qualifications, and confirm team positions and duties; during operations, use briefings and checklists to align understanding, advance according to procedures and the chain of command while continuously syncing the situation, and when deviations occur, first determine whether they fall within the authorized and procedural scope, then escalate to higher headquarters or the specialty position according to the chain of command; after the mission, review the process and results, organize operation and training records, and hand over outstanding items; at the same time take on checking personnel specialty training, qualifications, and standards compliance, and, within the authorized scope, pass on procedures to new members. The emphasis differs greatly by specialty: reconnaissance and target acquisition stress information verification and reporting standards, engineering and breaching stress equipment status and operating sequence, chemical defense and protection stress detection and handling levels, air defense and electronic related specialties stress system status and identification rules, and special operations support stresses interfaces and coordination.

entries.answer: This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 55-2013.00 “First-Line Supervisors of All Other Tactical Operations Specialists” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation): supervise and coordinate the activities of all other tactical operations specialists not separately classified in a dedicated category; supervisors may also perform the same tasks as the personnel they supervise. Based on this official definition, daily work includes: checking the mission description and specialty equipment and equipment status before the mission and confirming team composition according to personnel specialty and qualifications; aligning understanding through briefings and checklists and assigning team positions and duties; advancing according to procedures and the chain of command and continuously tracking the situation and recording key milestones during operations; when deviations occur, first determining whether they are within the procedural and authorized scope and then escalating to higher headquarters or the specialty position according to the chain of command; after the mission, reviewing the process and results, organizing operation and training records, and completing the handover; and at the same time organizing or taking part in specialty training and refresher training and verifying personnel specialty qualifications and standards compliance. This occupation is a U.S. military occupation and O*NET does not collect its data, so this page has no task list or work context percentages to cite.
entries.question: What do First-Line Supervisors of All Other Tactical Operations Specialists mainly do?

entries.answer: The supervision target and main outputs differ: this occupation's main output is the team supervision of all other tactical operations specialists not elsewhere classified, and it may personally perform the same tasks; first-line supervisors of weapons specialists / air crew members supervise weapons specialists and air crew members; first-line supervisors of air crew members supervise aviation air crew members; special forces have the execution of special operations missions as their main output; infantry and artillery and missile crew members and armored assault vehicle crew members have the tactical execution of their own specialty as their main output; command and control center specialists focus on operating and supporting command and control systems; and emergency management directors focus on plans and resource coordination.

subject.summary: Supervise and coordinate the activities of all other tactical operations specialists not separately classified in a dedicated category, and may personally perform the same tasks as the personnel they supervise: includes pre-mission preparation and briefings, assigning team positions and duties according to specialty and qualifications, on-scene supervision and coordination during operations, anomaly determination and escalation within authorization, post-mission review and records and handover, and checking personnel specialty training, qualifications, and standards compliance. The specific establishment, rank, duties, and authorization follow the rules of the service and unit concerned.
